output.review_comment:
The new logic maps to a coherent, generally-recognized title-case algorithm (preserve intentional mixed-case/acronyms, always capitalize first and last words, capitalize the word following a colon, lowercase minor words elsewhere) rather than hard-coding behavior for specific literal test inputs, so I don't see evidence of test-specific hacking. The switch from `.capitalize()` to explicit `word[0].upper() + word[1:].lower()` is functionally equivalent for normal words but correctly avoids clobbering already-capitalized internal letters when combined with the mixed-case guard.

I couldn't independently run the test suite or see the exact docstring wording in this review, so I'm trusting the PR author's claim that all 9 tests pass and that the rules were derived from the docstring — that's worth a quick sanity check before merge (`pytest` locally) since I can't verify it here.

Two non-blocking nits worth a follow-up:
1. `is_after_colon = ":" in words[index - 1]` uses substring containment rather than checking that the colon is at the end of the previous word (e.g. `words[index-1].endswith(":")`). A token like `"3:30"` would spuriously trigger colon-based capitalization of the next word. Probably harmless for the current test corpus, but slightly fragile.
2. The capitalization expression `word[0].upper() + word[1:].lower() if len(word) > 1 else word.upper()` is duplicated in the Rule 2 and Rule 3 branches; pulling it into a small helper (`_capitalize_word`) would reduce duplication and make future changes easier.

Neither issue blocks merging given the scope of the task (make the failing suite pass per docstring semantics), but flagging for a quick follow-up.
